{{Short description|Numerical method for calculating the gamma function}}In mathematics, '''Spouge's approximation''' is a formula for computing an approximation of the [[gamma function]]. It was named after John L. Spouge, who defined the formula in a 1994 paper.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Spouge | first1 = John L. | title = Computation of the Gamma, Digamma, and Trigamma Functions | doi = 10.1137/0731050 | journal = SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis | volume = 31 | issue = 3 | pages = 931–944 | year = 1994 |jstor = 2158038| url = https://zenodo.org/record/1236136 }}</ref> The formula is a modification of [[Stirling's approximation]], and has the form

:<math>\Gamma(z+1) = (z+a)^{z+\frac12} e^{-z-a} \left( c_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{a-1} \frac{c_k}{z+k} + \varepsilon_a(z) \right)</math>

where ''a'' is an arbitrary positive integer and the coefficients are given by

:<math>\begin{align} c_0 &= \sqrt{2 \pi}\\
c_k &= \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} (-k+a)^{k-\frac12} e^{-k+a} \qquad k\in\{1,2,\dots, a-1\}. \end{align}</math>

Spouge has proved that, if Re(''z'')&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 and ''a''&nbsp;>&nbsp;2, the relative error in discarding ''ε''<sub>''a''</sub>(''z'') is bounded by

:<math>a^{-\frac12} (2 \pi)^{-a-\frac12}.</math>

The formula is similar<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Causley | first1 = Matthew F. | title = The gamma function via interpolation | journal = Numerical Algorithms | volume = 90 | issue = 2 | pages = 687–707 | year = 2022 | url = https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1007/s11075-021-01204-8 }}</ref> to the [[Lanczos approximation]], but has some distinct features<ref>{{cite thesis | last=Pugh | first=Glendon | year=2004 | degree=PhD | url=http://web.mala.bc.ca/pughg/phdThesis/phdThesis.pdf | title=An analysis of the Lanczos Gamma approximation
}}</ref>. Whereas the Lanczos formula exhibits faster convergence <ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Johansson | first1 = Fredrik | title = Arbitrary precision computation of the gamma function | journal = Maple Transactions | volume = 3 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–51 | year = 2023 | url = https://inria.hal.science/hal-03346642/document }}</ref>, Spouge's coefficients are much easier to calculate and the error can be set arbitrarily low. The formula is therefore feasible for [[arbitrary-precision arithmetic|arbitrary-precision]]<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Lang | first1 = Johannes | last2 = Bernhard | first2 = Frank | title = Fast logarithmic Fourier-Laplace transform of nonintegrable functions | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 100 | year = 2019 | url=https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.100.053302 }}</ref> evaluation of the gamma function <ref>{{cite blog | last=Szewczyk | first=Kamila | year=2022 | url=https://iczelia.net/blog/factorial-approx/
| title=On factorial function approximation
}}</ref>.  However, special care must be taken to use sufficient precision when computing the sum due to the large size of the coefficients ''c<sub>k</sub>'', as well as their alternating sign. For example, for ''a''&nbsp;=&nbsp;49, one must compute the sum using about 65 decimal digits of precision in order to obtain the promised 40 decimal digits of accuracy.

Spouge's approximation for the scalar Gamma function, along with the Lanczos and Stirling approximations, generalizes to the matrix Gamma function <ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Cardoso | first1 = Joao R. | last2 = Sadeghi | first2 = Amir | title = Computation of matrix gamma function | journal =  BIT Numerical Mathematics | volume = 59 | pages = 343–370 | year = 2019 | url = https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10543-018-00744-1 }}</ref>.
